entities.summary:
Ralph Drengot, a Norman adventurer of the early 11th century, was a pivotal, albeit short-lived, figure in the initial Norman incursions into Southern Italy, a region then a contested mosaic of Lombard principalities, Byzantine territories, and nascent Papal influence. Born into a lesser Norman noble family, the Drengots, his actions, alongside his brothers Osmond, Gilbert, Asclettin, and Ranulf, inaugurated a new epoch of military and political transformation in the Mediterranean. His involvement, though brief, set the stage for the dramatic rise of Norman power that would culminate in the establishment of the Kingdom of Sicily and fundamentally reshape the geopolitical landscape of medieval Europe.

Following a violent incident in Normandy where his brother Osmond murdered a courtier of Duke Richard II, Ralph and his kinsmen were compelled to flee their homeland around 1016. Seeking fortune and expiation, they embarked on a pilgrimage to Monte Sant'Angelo sul Gargano in Apulia, a journey that swiftly transmuted into military service. They initially offered their martial prowess to the Lombard prince Melus of Bari, who was then in rebellion against Byzantine authority. Ralph participated in the Battle of Cannae in 1018, a devastating defeat for the Lombard-Norman forces against the Byzantines under Emperor Basil II's general, Boioannes, which scattered the early Norman contingents and underscored the precariousness of their position.
